content: As of April 2007, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) had developed a watt balance capable of achieving a combined relative standard uncertainty (CRSU) of 36 micrograms at a 68% confidence level, along with a short-term resolution of 10–15 micrograms. Ultimately, the watt balance was intended to redefine the kilogram in terms of the Planck constant, a fundamental physical constant that relates the energy of photons to their frequency. The advantage of electronic realizations like the watt balance is that the definition and dissemination of the kilogram would no longer depend on the stability of physical kilogram prototypes, which require meticulous handling and storage. This approach would eliminate the need for physicists to rely on assumptions about the stability of these prototypes, including those manufactured using atom-counting techniques. Instead, mass standards that are carefully calibrated and documented could be used, with their values expressed as one kilogram plus an offset. By employing such scales, the kilogram would not only be defined in electrical terms but also delineated in electrical terms. Mass artifacts calibrated using a watt balance would effectively serve as transfer standards. Additionally, the gravitational acceleration term, which is a critical factor in all scale-based realizations, is currently measured using absolute gravimeters. These devices utilize a dropping-mass method and incorporate an iodine-stabilized helium-neon laser interferometer. The fringe signal and frequency sweep output from the interferometer are measured with a rubidium atomic clock. Consequently, the gravitational term in the definition of an all-electronic kilogram would also be measured relative to natural invariants. Watt balances also allow for greater flexibility in selecting materials with desirable properties for mass standards. This could reduce relative uncertainty when making mass comparisons in air. Alternatively, entirely different materials and constructions could be explored to produce mass standards with enhanced stability. For example, osmium-iridium alloys could be investigated as alternatives if platinum's tendency to absorb hydrogen (due to its catalytic interaction with volatile organic compounds and hydrocarbon-based cleaning solvents) and atmospheric mercury were found to contribute to instability. Protective ceramic coatings, such as nitrides applied via vapor deposition, could also be evaluated for their ability to isolate these new alloys. The challenges associated with watt balances extend beyond reducing their uncertainty; they also involve making them practical realizations of the kilogram. Nearly every aspect of watt balances and their supporting equipment demands extraordinarily precise and accurate, state-of-the-art technology. Unlike devices such as atomic clocks, the complexity and cost of watt balances mean that only a limited number of countries would currently choose to fund their operation.
